facts.statement: The dinosaur Hypselospinus was first described by Richard Lydekker in 1889 as a species of Iguanodon.
facts.quote: Hypselospinus is a genus of iguanodontian dinosaur which was first described as a species of Iguanodon (I. fittoni) by Richard Lydekker in 1889

facts.statement: The specific name 'fittoni' honors William Henry Fitton, who worked in Early Cretaceous strata in England.
facts.quote: The species name honouring William Henry Fitton who had worked in the Early Cretaceous strata of England

facts.statement: The type specimen was found in Shornden Quarry, located over a distance of 50 yards.
facts.quote: The first of these specimens, NHMUK R.1635, was found in Shornden Quarry over distance of 50 yard

facts.statement: David Norman reclassified the fossils as the separate genus Hypselospinus in May 2010.
facts.quote: In May 2010 the fossils comprising Hypselospinus were by David Norman reclassified as a separate genus

facts.statement: Hypselospinus lived during the lower Valanginian stage, approximately 140 million years ago.
facts.quote: Hypselospinus lived during the lower Valanginian stage, around 140 million years ago

facts.statement: The time range for Hypselospinus spans from the Berriasian to the Valanginian, between 139.1 and 132.6 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Berriasian to Valanginian (139.1 to 132.6 million years ago)

facts.statement: Remains were discovered in the Lower Cretaceous Wadhurst Clay of Shornden, East Sussex, England.
facts.quote: The species Iguanodon fittoni was described from remains discovered in 1886 alongside an unnamed ichthyosaur in the lower Valanginian-age Lower Cretaceous Wadhurst Clay of Shornden, East Sussex, England

facts.statement: Hypselospinus was a lightly built iguanodontian estimated to be 6 meters long.
facts.quote: Hypselospinus was a lightly built iguanodontian estimated at 6 metres (19.7 ft) long

facts.statement: Hypselospinus belongs to the parent group Neoiguanodontia.
Hypselospinus is classified within the class Ornithischia.
It is debated whether I. hollingtoniensis should be included within I. fittoni, with some researchers retaining it as a separate species.
facts.quote: Not all authors agreed on the inclusion of I. hollingtoniensis within I. fittoni, with American palaeontologist Gregory S. Paul in 2008, and British palaeontologist Peter M. Galton in 2009 retaining the species as separate

facts.statement: A group of scientists independently reclassified I. fittoni into the genus Wadhurstia, making it a junior synonym of Hypselospinus.
facts.quote: Later that same year, a second group of scientists independently re-classified I. fittoni into a new genus they named Wadhurstia, which thus is a junior objective synonym of Hypselospinus
